title: Given an array containing only three distinct values (for example 0, 1, and 2), sort it in place in a single pass without using a counting approach or a library sort. (LeetCode: Sort Colors)
shortTitle: Dutch National Flag Problem (Three-Way Partition, Sort Colors)
keyPoints: The Dutch National Flag partitions an array of three values into three contiguous groups in a single pass
Three pointers: low (boundary of smallest), mid (scanner), high (boundary of largest)
Swap smallest values to the low region and largest values to the high region, leaving middle values in place
The asymmetry in pointer movement is the crux: mid advances after a low-swap but stays after a high-swap
Each step either advances mid or shrinks high, guaranteeing O(n) time and O(1) space
This is the three-way partition used inside three-way quicksort for duplicate-heavy arrays
The counting alternative takes two passes and overwrites values instead of moving objects

s1_definition.oneliner: Three pointers, one pass: send lows to the front, highs to the back, and let middles settle in the middle.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Dutch National Flag** – an in-place partitioning algorithm that sorts an array of three distinct values into three contiguous groups in a single linear pass.
- **Three pointers** – `low` marks the end of the smallest-value region, `high` marks the start of the largest-value region, and `mid` scans the unknown portion.
- **Invariant** – everything before `low` is the smallest value, between `low` and `mid` is the middle value, `mid` to `high` is unknown, and after `high` is the largest value.
- **Asymmetry** – after swapping to low, both `low` and `mid` advance; after swapping to high, only `high` moves because the incoming value is unexamined.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh at the National Bank of India has a pile of settlement slips each marked with one of three risk levels: low, medium, or high. He wants them grouped as all low first, then all medium, then all high, in one sweep. He keeps a left boundary for the next low slip, a right boundary for the next high slip, and his hand scans the middle. When his hand finds a low slip he tosses it to the left boundary, when it finds a high slip he tosses it to the right boundary, and when it finds a medium slip he leaves it and moves on.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Dutch National Flag: Three Regions

  ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬──────────┐
  │  Smallest │  Middle   │  Unknown      │  Largest  │
  │  (0)      │  (1)      │              │  (2)      │
  └──────────┴──────────┴──────────────┴──────────┘
  0         low        mid             high       n-1

  Actions:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ arr[mid] == 0 → swap(low, mid), low++, mid++ │
  │ arr[mid] == 1 → mid++                         │
  │ arr[mid] == 2 → swap(mid, high), high--       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Key: mid advances after low-swap (safe)
       mid stays after high-swap (unexamined value)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Dutch National Flag problem asks you to sort an array of three distinct values into three contiguous groups in a single pass using three pointers and constant space. The naive counting alternative works, but the three-pointer method is what demonstrates real command of in-place partitioning.

The low boundary and mid scanner start at the front, the high boundary at the end. Everything before low is the smallest value, everything after high is the largest, and mid to high is still unexamined. You look at the element under mid: smallest swaps to the low boundary with both pointers advancing, largest swaps to the high boundary with only high moving, and middle values just advance mid.

The asymmetry in pointer movement is the crux and where almost everyone introduces a bug. After a low-swap, the element that arrives at mid was already scanned, so advancing is safe. After a high-swap, the element that arrives is unexamined, so mid must stay put. Being able to explain exactly why is what separates understanding from memorization.

In the National Bank of India, the risk engine used this to reorder a large settlement queue by risk tier so operations could clear safe items fast and focus on the risky tail. The same partition step appears inside three-way quicksort, handling duplicate-heavy arrays efficiently.

Remember one sentence: three pointers, one pass, and the asymmetry on the high-swap is the entire trick.
